pll1d26c3-d1e3501.summary: States that not all said of God is said according to substance: some is said by relation, which is not an accident because not mutable.
claims: Some predicates of God are relative.
Relations in God are not accidents.

pll1d26c3-d1e3504.summary: Cites De Trinitate V: nothing is said of God by accident, since nothing in him is changeable or losable, yet not all is said by substance. Father and Son are said relatively, which is not accidental, since the Father is always Father and the Son always born. If the Son began or ceased to be Son, it would be accidental; since each is said only in relation to the other, it is not substance, but it is eternal and unchangeable.
claims: Nothing is said of God accidentally.
Not everything is said of God substantially.
Father and Son are said relatively, eternally, and unchangeably.

pll1d26c3-d1e3525.summary: Draws out: some things are said of God by substance, some by relation, nothing by accident. The Father's property is that he has a Son, the Son's that he has a Father, and these properties are eternal and immutable, since the Father is always Father and the Son always Son.
claims: The Father's property is having a Son; the Son's is having a Father.
These properties are eternal and immutable.

pll1d26c3-d1e3529.summary: Cites Hilary, De Trinitate XII: if it is always proper to the Father to be Father, it must always be proper to the Son to be Son; where the Father is always, the Son is always, and one who is not always Father did not always beget.
claims: The Father is always Father, so the Son is always Son.

pll1d26c3-d1e3549.summary: Further Hilary: it is manifest that being Son is proper to God born.
claims: Being Son is proper to the begotten God.

pl-l1d26c3.summary: Explains that not everything said of God is said according to substance; some things are said by relation, which is not an accident, since not changeable. Augustine, De Trinitate V: nothing is said of God accidentally; Father and Son are said relatively to each other, not substantially, yet not accidentally, since the Father is always Father and the Son always Son. So the Father's property is to have the Son, the Son's to have the Father, eternal and immutable. Hilary confirms: if being Father is always proper to the Father, being Son is always proper to the Son.
claims: Some things are said of God by substance, others by relation, none by accident.
Relations in God are not accidents, since they are not changeable.
The Father is always Father and the Son always Son.
The Father's property is to have the Son; the Son's to have the Father.
These properties are eternal and immutable.
